cached_query: What is the difference between a debit card and a credit card?
cached_answer:
The core difference is whose money you are spending. A debit card is linked directly to your current account. When you tap it, the amount leaves your own balance within seconds, and if the balance is not there the payment is simply declined. There is no borrowing involved, so there is no interest to pay and no way to run up a debt on the card itself.

A credit card works the other way round. The issuer pays the merchant on your behalf and lends you the amount up to a pre-agreed credit limit. You then get a monthly statement; if you clear it in full by the due date you pay nothing extra, and if you do not, interest accrues on the outstanding balance. Because the card is genuinely a credit product, the issuer reports how you use it, so paying on time steadily builds a credit history that lenders later look at.

The third practical difference is what happens when something goes wrong. Money spent on a credit card is the issuer's money until you repay it, which is why disputed charges, undelivered goods and fraud are generally easier to reverse on a credit card. On a debit card the money is already gone from your account while the dispute is being investigated.

cached_answer:
Both codes are hardware sensor faults rather than software errors, and both clear themselves once the underlying condition is fixed.

E22 is the grinder code. It fires when the grinder motor draws more current than expected, which in practice means the burrs are jammed. The usual cause is oily dark-roast beans packing into the burr chamber. Turn the machine off at the wall socket, empty the bean hopper, brush the burr chamber out with the supplied brush, and power it back on. The code clears after one successful grind.

The right answer depends on what you are defending against, and on public Wi-Fi the thing you are defending against is the network itself.

A VPN builds an encrypted tunnel from your device to a server you choose. They cannot read the contents, and they cannot see which sites you visit. That is a direct answer to the public Wi-Fi threat model.

First, only that application is covered; everything else on the device still goes out in the clear. Second, most proxies do no encryption of their own, so the network operator still sees the request contents.

So for privacy on an untrusted network, a VPN is the correct choice and a proxy is not a substitute. A proxy earns its place elsewhere: making one application appear to be somewhere else, on a network you already trust.

cached_query: Should I use a VPN or a proxy to stay private on public Wi-Fi?
cached_answer:
Use a VPN. It encrypts everything leaving the device and hides both the sites and the contents from whoever runs the access point, which is the actual public Wi-Fi threat. A proxy covers only one configured application and usually adds no encryption at all, so it does not address that threat; it is a geo-shifting tool for networks you already trust.

Some adjacent dimensions worth knowing:

Speed. A VPN adds a hop and encryption overhead, typically costing 10-30 percent of throughput and a few milliseconds of latency. A proxy adds a hop but no crypto, so it is usually faster.

Logging. Both move your trust rather than removing it - you stop trusting the cafe and start trusting the VPN or proxy operator. A published no-logs policy that has been independently audited is the only meaningful distinction between providers.

DNS leaks. A badly configured VPN client can still send DNS queries over the local network, which reveals every domain you visit. Check for DNS leaks after setting one up.

Corporate split tunnelling. Work VPNs often route only company traffic through the tunnel and everything else directly, which means they do not protect your personal browsing on that cafe network at all.

cached_query: What are the two main types of solar panel used on home roofs?
cached_answer:
Almost every domestic rooftop installation uses one of two silicon panel types, and the choice between them is mostly a trade of roof area against price.

Monocrystalline panels are made from wafers cut from a single grown silicon crystal. Because the crystal lattice is continuous, electrons move through it with fewer obstacles, and efficiency lands around 20 to 23 percent. Visually they are uniformly black with rounded cell corners. The manufacturing process wastes a good deal of silicon, which is why they carry the higher price.

Polycrystalline panels are cast: molten silicon is poured into a mould and allowed to solidify into many crystals at once. The grain boundaries between those crystals impede electron flow slightly, so efficiency sits around 15 to 18 percent, and the panels have the familiar blue, speckled appearance. Very little silicon is wasted, so they are cheaper.

In practice that means monocrystalline wins when roof space is the constraint, and polycrystalline wins when budget is the constraint and there is plenty of unshaded roof to cover.

cached_query: Should I turn on two-factor authentication for my work email?
cached_answer:
Yes, and it is probably the single highest-value security change available to you.

The reason is what attacks on email accounts actually look like. Very few of them are a determined attacker targeting you specifically. The overwhelming majority are credential stuffing: someone takes a list of email addresses and passwords leaked from an unrelated breach and tries them, automatically, against every service they can. If you have ever reused that password, the attempt succeeds. Two-factor authentication breaks that whole class of attack, because the password on its own no longer opens the account.

Not all second factors are equal. An SMS code is much better than nothing, but it can be intercepted by a SIM-swap, where an attacker persuades your mobile carrier to move your number to their SIM. An authenticator app generates its codes on your device with no network involvement, so there is nothing for the carrier to hand over. Prefer the app.

The practical cost is small. Enabling it is a two-minute job in the account security settings, and after the initial setup most work systems only re-prompt on a new device or after a set period.

cached_query: What is the difference between a debit card and a credit card?
cached_answer:
The core difference is whose money you are spending. A debit card is linked directly to your current account. When you tap it, the amount leaves your own balance within seconds, and if the balance is not there the payment is simply declined. There is no borrowing involved, so there is no interest to pay and no way to run up a debt on the card itself.

A credit card works the other way round. The issuer pays the merchant on your behalf and lends you the amount up to a pre-agreed credit limit. You then get a monthly statement; if you clear it in full by the due date you pay nothing extra, and if you do not, interest accrues on the outstanding balance. Because the card is genuinely a credit product, the issuer reports how you use it, so paying on time steadily builds a credit history that lenders later look at.

The third practical difference is what happens when something goes wrong. Money spent on a credit card is the issuer's money until you repay it, which is why disputed charges, undelivered goods and fraud are generally easier to reverse on a credit card. On a debit card the money is already gone from your account while the dispute is being investigated.

Domestic roofs use two silicon panel types. Monocrystalline is cut from a single grown crystal, looks uniformly black, runs at about 20-23 percent efficiency and costs more. Polycrystalline is cast from many crystals at once, looks blue and speckled, runs at about 15-18 percent and costs less, so it needs more roof area for the same output.

Several further dimensions separate them:

Temperature coefficient. Output falls as panels heat up. Monocrystalline typically loses about 0.3 percent per degree above 25C, polycrystalline about 0.4, so the gap widens on a hot roof.

Warranty. Both are usually sold with a 25-year performance warranty, but monocrystalline products more often guarantee a higher end-of-term output figure.

Appearance on the roof. The uniform black of monocrystalline is much less visually obtrusive on a dark roof, which matters for planning consent in conservation areas.

Weight and roof load. Both sit around 18-20 kg per panel, so structural load is rarely the deciding factor between them.

cached_query: What are the two main types of solar panel used on home roofs?
cached_answer:
Almost every domestic rooftop installation uses one of two silicon panel types, and the choice between them is mostly a trade of roof area against price.

Monocrystalline panels are made from wafers cut from a single grown silicon crystal. Because the crystal lattice is continuous, electrons move through it with fewer obstacles, and efficiency lands around 20 to 23 percent. Visually they are uniformly black with rounded cell corners. The manufacturing process wastes a good deal of silicon, which is why they carry the higher price.

Polycrystalline panels are cast: molten silicon is poured into a mould and allowed to solidify into many crystals at once. The grain boundaries between those crystals impede electron flow slightly, so efficiency sits around 15 to 18 percent, and the panels have the familiar blue, speckled appearance. Very little silicon is wasted, so they are cheaper.

In practice that means monocrystalline wins when roof space is the constraint, and polycrystalline wins when budget is the constraint and there is plenty of unshaded roof to cover.

cached_query: Should I turn on two-factor authentication for my work email?
cached_answer:
Yes, and it is probably the single highest-value security change available to you.

The reason is what attacks on email accounts actually look like. Very few of them are a determined attacker targeting you specifically. The overwhelming majority are credential stuffing: someone takes a list of email addresses and passwords leaked from an unrelated breach and tries them, automatically, against every service they can. If you have ever reused that password, the attempt succeeds. Two-factor authentication breaks that whole class of attack, because the password on its own no longer opens the account.

Not all second factors are equal. An SMS code is much better than nothing, but it can be intercepted by a SIM-swap, where an attacker persuades your mobile carrier to move your number to their SIM. An authenticator app generates its codes on your device with no network involvement, so there is nothing for the carrier to hand over. Prefer the app.

The practical cost is small. Enabling it is a two-minute job in the account security settings, and after the initial setup most work systems only re-prompt on a new device or after a set period.
